## Background

This analysis uses patient metadata I retrieved from the NIH/NCI Genomic Data
Commons REST API during my MSc research project. The original project used the
imaging and report data; this analysis uses the clinical fields that came with
it, which include vital status, time to death and time to last follow-up across
32 TCGA project cohorts.

The aim is to model overall survival and to check whether the relationships
behave the way established oncology prognostic factors would predict. I am
treating the data as observational, because it is: these are not trial arms and
there is no randomised comparison here.

```{r libraries}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(survival)
library(survminer)
library(broom)

set.seed(42)
```

```{r paths}
# Created by fetch_metadata.py from the GDC API (see README.md).
metadata_path <- "data/metadata.csv"
```

## Loading and cleaning

GDC uses several different tokens for missing values, so they are all declared
up front rather than cleaned up later.

```{r load}
raw <- read_csv(
  metadata_path,
  na = c("", "NA", "'--", "--", "not reported", "Not Reported",
         "unknown", "Unknown", "Not Allowed To Collect")
)

nrow(raw)
n_distinct(raw$case_id)
```

The dataset is indexed by slide, and a patient can in principle contribute more
than one slide. Survival is a patient-level question, so analysing at slide
level would silently weight patients by how many slides they happen to have. I
checked rather than assumed: in this extract the two counts are equal, so the
deduplication below is a no-op. I have left it in because the file is keyed by
slide and the one-to-one relationship is a property of this particular extract
rather than something the schema guarantees.

```{r dedupe}
cases <- raw %>%
  arrange(case_id, slide_id) %>%
  distinct(case_id, .keep_all = TRUE)

nrow(cases)
```

## Constructing the survival object

Follow-up time comes from two different columns depending on whether the patient
died during follow-up. Patients still alive at last contact are right-censored.

```{r survprep}
dat <- cases %>%
  mutate(
    event = case_when(
      vital_status == "Dead"  ~ 1L,
      vital_status == "Alive" ~ 0L,
      TRUE ~ NA_integer_
    ),
    time_days = if_else(event == 1L,
                        as.numeric(days_to_death),
                        as.numeric(days_to_last_follow_up)),
    time_months = time_days / 30.44,

    # AJCC stage arrives as "Stage IIIA", "Stage IV" and similar.
    # Order matters here: case_when short-circuits, so IV is tested
    # before III, which is tested before II, before I.
    stage = case_when(
      str_detect(ajcc_pathologic_stage, "IV")  ~ "IV",
      str_detect(ajcc_pathologic_stage, "III") ~ "III",
      str_detect(ajcc_pathologic_stage, "II")  ~ "II",
      str_detect(ajcc_pathologic_stage, "I")   ~ "I",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    stage   = factor(stage, levels = c("I", "II", "III", "IV")),
    sex     = factor(gender),
    age     = as.numeric(age_at_index),
    cohort  = factor(project_id)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(event), !is.na(time_days), time_days > 0)

nrow(dat)
table(dat$event)
```

Cases with non-positive follow-up time are dropped. A recorded survival time of
zero or less is a data quality artefact rather than an instantaneous death, and
`Surv()` will not accept it.

```{r cohortsummary}
dat %>%
  group_by(cohort) %>%
  summarise(
    n       = n(),
    deaths  = sum(event),
    staged  = sum(!is.na(stage)),
    median_followup_months = round(median(time_months), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))
```

### Staging is missing by design, not at random

The `staged` column is worth pausing on. Roughly a third of the analysis set has
no AJCC stage, and the missingness is not spread evenly: entire cohorts have
none at all. That is not a data quality problem, it is a clinical one. AJCC
staging does not apply to several of these tumour types. Brain tumours (LGG,
GBM) are graded by WHO criteria rather than staged by TNM; gynaecological
cancers such as UCEC, OV and CESC are conventionally staged by FIGO; prostate
cancer in this release carries its own staging fields.

This matters because every model below that includes stage silently excludes
those cohorts. That drops the sample from 6,864 patients to 4,346 and removes
whole tumour types from the analysis rather than a random subset of patients.
Reporting the stage-adjusted hazard ratios without saying so would overstate
what the model covers, so the restricted sample is stated alongside each result.

## Kaplan-Meier estimates

```{r km-overall}
fit_overall <- survfit(Surv(time_months, event) ~ 1, data = dat)
fit_overall
```

Stratifying by AJCC stage. If the data behave sensibly, the curves should
separate in stage order, with Stage IV the worst.

```{r km-stage, fig.height=7}
stage_dat <- dat %>% filter(!is.na(stage))

fit_stage <- survfit(Surv(time_months, event) ~ stage, data = stage_dat)

ggsurvplot(
  fit_stage,
  data        = stage_dat,
  pval        = TRUE,
  conf.int    = TRUE,
  risk.table  = TRUE,
  xlab        = "Months since diagnosis",
  ylab        = "Overall survival probability",
  legend.title = "AJCC stage",
  palette     = "Dark2"
)
```

Median survival with confidence intervals, read off the same fit:

```{r km-medians}
round(
  summary(fit_stage)$table[, c("records", "events", "median", "0.95LCL", "0.95UCL")],
  1
)
```

The ordering is monotonic in stage, and the gap between Stage III and Stage IV
is far larger than any other adjacent pair, which is what the hazard ratios
below also show.

The upper confidence limit is `NA` for Stages I, II and III. That is not a
failure of the computation: the survival curve for those groups never drops far
enough below 0.5 within the observed follow-up for an upper bound on the median
to be estimated. The median itself is identified, but how much longer it could
plausibly be is not, and quoting the point estimate without that caveat would
imply more precision than the data support.

```{r logrank}
survdiff(Surv(time_months, event) ~ stage, data = stage_dat)
```

The log-rank test asks whether the survival distributions differ across stage
groups. It tells us the curves are not the same; it does not tell us by how
much, or in which direction, which is what the Cox model below is for.

## Cox proportional hazards model

```{r cox}
cox_dat <- stage_dat %>%
  filter(!is.na(age), !is.na(sex)) %>%
  mutate(cohort = droplevels(cohort))

cox_fit <- coxph(
  Surv(time_months, event) ~ age + sex + stage + strata(cohort),
  data = cox_dat
)

summary(cox_fit)
```

I stratify by cohort rather than adjusting for it. Different tumour types have
very different baseline hazards, and stratification lets each cohort keep its own
baseline while still estimating a shared effect for age, sex and stage. Treating
cohort as an ordinary covariate would force a single baseline hazard onto all 22
cohorts in the model, which is not a defensible assumption.

```{r cox-tidy}
tidy(cox_fit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

Coefficients are exponentiated, so they read as hazard ratios. A hazard ratio
above 1 means a higher instantaneous risk of death relative to the reference
level, which is Stage I for stage and the first factor level for sex.

### Checking the proportional hazards assumption

The Cox model assumes hazard ratios are constant over time. That assumption is
testable and is worth testing rather than asserting.

```{r phtest}
ph_test <- cox.zph(cox_fit)
ph_test
```

```{r phplot, fig.height=6}
plot(ph_test)
```

A small p-value for a term means its effect varies with time, in which case the
single hazard ratio reported above is an average over the follow-up period and
should not be quoted as if it were constant. The global test covers the model as
a whole.

## Logistic regression

A separate question, and a binary rather than time-to-event one: can we predict
whether a patient presented at an advanced stage from demographic information
alone?

```{r logistic}
log_dat <- cox_dat %>%
  mutate(advanced = as.integer(stage %in% c("III", "IV")))

logit_fit <- glm(advanced ~ age + sex, data = log_dat, family = binomial)

tidy(logit_fit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

```{r logistic-fitcheck}
log_dat$pred <- predict(logit_fit, type = "response")

# Calibration: observed rate within deciles of predicted risk.
log_dat %>%
  mutate(decile = ntile(pred, 10)) %>%
  group_by(decile) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_predicted = round(mean(pred), 3),
    observed_rate  = round(mean(advanced), 3),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

I check calibration rather than only discrimination because a model can rank
patients well and still produce probabilities that are systematically wrong. If
the mean predicted risk in each decile does not track the observed rate, the
model is miscalibrated even if it separates cases adequately.

Here the result is negative, and worth reporting as such. Both coefficients
reach significance, but predicted risk spans only about 0.25 to 0.42 across the
whole cohort, and the observed rate does not increase monotonically across
deciles: the top decile sits below the eighth. Age and sex carry a real but very
weak signal for stage at presentation, and a model built on them alone is not
usable for anything. That is a sensible clinical finding rather than a
disappointing one, since stage at diagnosis depends on tumour biology,
screening access and time to presentation rather than on demographics. It is
also a reminder that statistical significance and practical usefulness are
different questions: with roughly four thousand patients, a trivial effect will
clear p < 0.001 comfortably.

## Limitations

Worth stating explicitly, since these constrain what the results above can
support:

- This is observational data from a tissue repository, not a clinical trial.
  There is no randomisation and no controlled comparison, so none of the
  estimates here are causal.
- Treatment information in these fields is sparse, so the models are
  unadjusted for therapy, which is a substantial confounder for survival.
- Follow-up duration varies considerably between cohorts, and cohorts with
  short follow-up contribute few events.
- Stage was collapsed from the AJCC sub-stages, which discards information
  within each stage group.
- Deduplication to one row per case keeps the first slide per patient. The
  clinical fields are patient-level so this does not bias the clinical data,
  but it is an arbitrary choice worth recording.
